raw_text:
- The objective is to investigate and explain the persistent completion-time differences between sites with identical nominal work processes.
- The scope includes understanding measurable factors contributing to these differences and distinguishing among potential explanations through empirical observations.

Assumptions
- Sites using the same nominal work process operate under similar environmental constraints.
- Completion times are influenced by measurable aspects of the work process and worker performance.

Research design
- Quasi-experimental design: Select sites with identical nominal work processes and measure completion times under various conditions.
- Pretest-posttest control group design: One group undergoes an intervention (process optimization) while another continues as usual to assess the impact on completion times.

Data or evidence needed
- Baseline completion times for each site under normal conditions.
- Completion times after implementing a purported improvement in the work process.
- Observational data on specific activities during the completion of tasks.
- Worker performance metrics (e.g., error rate, speed) before and after process changes.

Measurement
- Completion time for tasks as the primary metric.
- Quality of completion as a secondary metric: Accuracy, adherence to standards, and customer satisfaction.
- Observational checklists to record specific activities performed.

Analysis
- General linear models (GLMs) to analyze the effect of the intervention on completion times.
- Regression analysis to understand relationships among measurable factors (e.g., time spent on specific tasks, worker performance metrics).
- Chi-square tests to explore any association between observed activities and completion times.

Decision / stopping rule
- Simple effects tests to check whether the intervention effect is due to changes in measurable factors.
- Significance levels of p < 0.05 for both the main and interaction effects.
- Sample size requirement: 20 sites to ensure statistical power.

Limitations
- External factors (e.g., sudden changes in demand, staff turnover) may confound the results.
- Self-reported performance metrics may introduce bias.
- Potential for placebo or Hawthorne effects, resulting from the awareness of being part of an experiment.

[End of research plan]
